genZNote: Raw oysters plus a cut on your leg is exactly the combination this organism is waiting for.

habitat.naturalHabitat: Warm coastal seawater and brackish estuarine water
habitat.hostAssociation: Not a human commensal; acquired via seafood consumption or wound exposure to seawater
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Concentrates in filter-feeding shellfish (especially oysters) from warm coastal waters, particularly in summer months

culture.media: TCBS (thiosulfate-citrate-bile salts-sucrose) agar, blood agar with added salt
culture.growthCharacteristics: Halophilic — requires or strongly prefers a salt-supplemented medium; facultative anaerobe
culture.colonyMorphology: Green colonies on TCBS agar (sucrose non-fermenter, unlike V. cholerae)

biochemicalTests.result: Halophilic — grows best with added salt

identificationClues: Green (sucrose-negative) colonies on TCBS agar, distinguishing it from the yellow (sucrose-fermenting) colonies of V. cholerae
Rapid, severe wound infections after seawater exposure, or septicemia after raw shellfish (especially oyster) consumption
Particularly severe/fatal in patients with liver disease or iron overload conditions (e.g., hemochromatosis)

diseases: Severe wound infections/cellulitis, which can progress rapidly to necrotizing fasciitis
Primary septicemia after ingestion of raw or undercooked shellfish, especially oysters
virulenceFactors: Polysaccharide capsule — antiphagocytic, key to bloodstream survival
Cytolysin/hemolysin toxins contributing to tissue necrosis
Enhanced iron acquisition — explains markedly increased severity in patients with iron overload (e.g., hemochromatosis) or chronic liver disease
clinicalImportance.transmission: Ingestion of raw/undercooked shellfish (especially oysters) or wound exposure to warm seawater
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: One of the most lethal foodborne pathogens by case-fatality rate for septicemia, particularly in patients with underlying liver disease; incidence rising with warming coastal waters
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: A rapidly progressive wound infection or sepsis following seawater exposure or raw shellfish consumption should prompt urgent consideration of V. vulnificus, especially in a patient with liver disease

examFacts.keyBiochemicalReaction: Oxidase positive, sucrose non-fermenter on TCBS (green colonies)
examFacts.importantDisease: Necrotizing wound infection and fulminant septicemia after raw oyster consumption
examFacts.importantTest: TCBS agar (green, sucrose-negative colonies); history of seawater/shellfish exposure is a key clinical clue
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: A halophilic Vibrio causing rapidly fatal septicemia in patients with liver disease/iron overload after raw oyster consumption or seawater wound exposure
